analysis.one_liner: Gives federal inspectors power to order recalls of contaminated meat, poultry, and food and fine violators.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2002 with two cosponsors and never received a committee hearing, a floor vote, or any other action before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal food safety law so that any company in the meat, poultry, or general food supply that had reason to believe a product was contaminated or mislabeled had to tell the Agriculture Department, and the Secretary could stop distribution and order a recall if the company did not act. It would also let the Secretary pull federal inspectors out of plants with willful or repeated violations and levy civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation per day against meat and poultry plants, and up to $500,000 against companies for other food, until the violation was fixed. At the time, the government could ask companies to recall tainted food but had no power to force a recall.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy meat, poultry, and packaged food. Faster, mandatory recalls and daily fines would give companies a financial reason to catch contamination early and pull tainted products from shelves quickly, instead of negotiating the pace of a voluntary recall with the government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shoppers of meat and packaged food

how_it_helps.text: Any person in the supply chain, other than a household consumer, who has reason to believe meat, poultry, or food is adulterated or misbranded must notify the Secretary as soon as practicable [S3].

If the Secretary finds a product is adulterated or misbranded and a reasonable probability that eating it threatens public health, the Secretary must first offer companies the chance to stop distribution and recall; if they do not act in the required time and manner, the Secretary can order the stop-distribution and notification by mandatory order [S3].
The Secretary can require recall with a timetable after a hearing held within two business days, and can direct that consumers who may have received the product be notified [S3].

The Secretary may refuse or withdraw inspection from an establishment whose responsible people committed willful or repeated violations, and may suspend inspection pending an expedited hearing when needed to protect consumer health [S3].

The Secretary may assess civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation for meat and poultry (each day a violation continues is a separate offense) and up to $100,000 per act for individuals or $500,000 for companies for other foods, with amounts scaled to gravity, culpability, business size, and violation history; unpaid penalties can be collected by the Attorney General in court and inspection can be withheld until payment [S3].

Distributors and retailers that are notified of a contamination finding must immediately stop distributing the product, which keeps a recalled item from sitting on shelves while the recall proceeds [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors, food manufacturers, distributors, and retailers, who would bear the cost of faster recalls, the $100,000-per-violation-per-day fines for continued violations, the risk of losing federal inspection, and new record-keeping duties to show the government where a product went.

drawbacks.text: The notification duty falls on every person in the supply chain except household consumers, so even small distributors and retailers could face orders and penalties for problems originating upstream at a processor [S3].

The bill lets the Secretary treat a civil penalty as adequate in place of prosecution whenever the Secretary believes the public interest is served, which a critic could read as allowing serious violations to be settled with fines [S3].

Recall costs and per-day fines are ultimately business costs, so some portion would be passed to consumers in prices, and broad discretion vested in the Secretary could be applied unevenly across firms of different sizes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core exchange is straightforward: faster mandatory recalls of contaminated food versus higher compliance and recall costs for food companies. The consumer benefit is direct — contaminated meat and poultry sickens people, and the gap between a voluntary request and a mandatory order is time during which tainted food keeps moving. The design has real soft spots (supply-chain-wide liability, fines substituting for prosecution), but the main cost falls on the industry being regulated rather than on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee in July 2002, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Harkin introduced the bill on July 26, 2002, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind: no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote appears in the action history before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].
The bill died in committee, so none of its recall, inspection-withdrawal, or civil-penalty provisions took effect [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors and food companies are better off: they never faced mandatory recall orders, withdrawal of federal inspection, or fines of up to $100,000 per violation per day. Consumers gained nothing, because the government's recall power over contaminated food remained voluntary.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFER Meat, Poultry, and Food Act and referred it to the Agriculture Committee.

for.name: Sen. Kent Conrad
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Dakota; cosponsor

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 26, 2002 and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed giving USDA mandatory recall and penalty authority over meat and poultry plants, arguing voluntary recalls work.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; both the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the two cosponsors were the only Senate Democrats to sign on.

industries.note: The bill would have given the Agriculture Secretary mandatory recall authority over adulterated meat and poultry, power to pull federal inspectors from repeat-violation plants, and fines up to $100,000 per violation per day. The industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against consumers, who bore the risk of contaminated products staying on shelves during voluntary recalls.

The bill extended the same notification and mandatory recall scheme to all food under the food and drug laws, with penalties up to $500,000 per act for companies, and required notified distributors to stop selling the product immediately. Faster recalls protect shoppers but impose recall and compliance costs across the supply chain.
